newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Bildt names supervisor for Brcko, vows action.
newsitem.headline: Bildt names supervisor for Brcko, vows action.

text.p: Carl Bildt, the West's chief representative in Bosnia, said on Friday that efforts to resolve a territorial dispute over the town of Brcko, which has cast a shadow over the Bosnian peace process, would be stepped up.
Bildt appointed a senior U.S. diplomat, Bill Farrand, as supervisor for the Bosnian town, and said the presence of international police monitors in the area would be increased.

Speaking after a high-level international conference on Brcko's future in Vienna's imperial Hofburg palace, Bildt told a news conference: "A robust presence of international police monitors is necessary to promote respect for freedom of movement and to facilitate the orderly return of refugees."
He said the number of police monitors in the area, which is claimed by both Serbs and the Muslim-Croat federation, would be increased by more than 200.
"Of all of the human rights violence that we see roughly half is done by the police, the other half is tolerated by local police. When we have a (monitor) there, they behave."

Brcko was captured by Bosnian Serbs early in the 1992-95 war and purged of its mainly Moslem-Croat pre-war population. The Serbs threatened to resume the war if they were denied control of Brcko, which sits on a narrow land corridor linking eastern and western Serb-controlled territories.
Moslems and Croats in turn claim Serb control over Brcko would reward so-called ethnic cleansing and deprive them of access to the Sava and Danube rivers and other key waterways.
U.S arbiter Robert Owen three weeks ago ruled that the Sava river port town would be put under international supervision pending a final decision next year on its status.
Bildt hinted that the Serb side in particular was not too happy about the Brcko agreement. "They want either more or less. We did not ask for any specific reaction," he said.
Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic told Reuters the significance of the deal should not be overplayed. "I cannot say that this is something very special," she said.
Farrand, a career diplomat with experience in eastern Europe, said the road to lasting peace in Brcko could be rocky and warned his new job would not be an easy one.
"I come to this complex task with a sense of humility. I only hope that 30 years in the diplomatic service will prepare me for some of the difficult tasks we face," he said.

Farrand is charged with strengthening democratic institutions and overseeing implementation of the Dayton peace accord that ended Bosnia's 43-month war but was almost derailed by the Brcko issue. He will also oversee the return of refugees, ensure freedom of movement and implement economic reconstruction.
The Vienna conference, attended by all key players in the Bosnian peace process, agreed that economic assistance to the region was vital to ensure lasting peace.
"It is crucial that we contribute to the economic revival of the area, which is heavily devastated. We need a lot of money," Bildt said.
In a barely veiled criticism of the Vienna agreement, Bosnian Foreign Minister Ejup Ganic said the programme lacked sufficiently detailed proposals.

"There will be more police, more money, and there's a commitment to opening the roads, but we'll have to see. I wanted more progress, more specifics, more dates, but I couldn't push too much," he told Reuters.
